```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(bayesDP)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%", fig.align = "center", dpi = 150)
```

# Purpose and inputs

`bdpnormal()` estimates a population mean from a sample mean, sample standard deviation, and sample size. With two arms, the effect is the treatment mean minus the control mean. Specify the outcome units and which direction represents benefit.

Supply each source as a `(mu, sigma, N)` triplet: `sigma` is the sample SD, not a standard error. The suffixes `_t`, `_c`, `0_t`, and `0_c` identify the four current/historical and treatment/control sources. Current treatment is required; controls may be current, historical, or both. Means and variances must be estimated from at least two observations with positive SDs.

See the [borrowing overview](borrowing.html) for the shared methodology. The examples select `method = "fixed"` explicitly; `"mc"` is the default.

# One-arm example

The current study has mean 45, SD 10, and 50 participants. The historical study has mean 50, SD 10, and 50 participants. For this illustration, regard the outcome as a continuous score in the same units in both studies.

```{r one-arm-fits}
set.seed(42)
current_only <- bdpnormal(
  mu_t = 45, sigma_t = 10, N_t = 50,
  mu0_t = 50, sigma0_t = 10, N0_t = 50,
  method = "fixed", fix_alpha = TRUE, alpha_max = 0
)
set.seed(42)
discounted <- bdpnormal(
  mu_t = 45, sigma_t = 10, N_t = 50,
  mu0_t = 50, sigma0_t = 10, N0_t = 50,
  method = "fixed", fix_alpha = FALSE, alpha_max = 1
)
set.seed(42)
full_borrowing <- bdpnormal(
  mu_t = 45, sigma_t = 10, N_t = 50,
  mu0_t = 50, sigma0_t = 10, N0_t = 50,
  method = "fixed", fix_alpha = TRUE, alpha_max = 1
)
fits <- list("Current only" = current_only, "Discounted" = discounted,
  "Full borrowing" = full_borrowing)
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, function(fit) {
  arm <- fit$posterior_treatment
  c(alpha = arm$alpha_discount, median = median(arm$posterior_mu),
    lower = unname(quantile(arm$posterior_mu, 0.025)),
    upper = unname(quantile(arm$posterior_mu, 0.975)))
}))
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4,
  col.names = c("Historical weight", "Median mean", "Lower 95% CrI", "Upper 95% CrI"))
```

The estimated historical weight is `r round(discounted$posterior_treatment$alpha_discount, 4)`, so the posterior median mean, `r round(median(discounted$posterior_treatment$posterior_mu), 4)`, remains close to the current sample mean. With full borrowing the median is `r round(median(full_borrowing$posterior_treatment$posterior_mu), 4)`, approximately halfway between 45 and 50 in this equal-size, equal-SD example. With unequal variances, the sources have different precisions, so full borrowing need not give the sample-size-weighted mean.

```{r mean-posteriors, fig.cap="Posterior distributions of the population mean. Estimated borrowing is small because the current and historical means differ relative to their precision.", fig.alt="Posterior distributions of the population mean. Estimated borrowing is small because the current and historical means differ relative to their precision."}
plot(discounted, type = "posteriors")
```

# Two-arm example

Add current and historical control groups with mean 40, SD 10, and 50 participants each.

```{r two-arm-fit}
set.seed(42)
fit_two <- bdpnormal(
  mu_t = 45, sigma_t = 10, N_t = 50,
  mu0_t = 50, sigma0_t = 10, N0_t = 50,
  mu_c = 40, sigma_c = 10, N_c = 50,
  mu0_c = 40, sigma0_c = 10, N0_c = 50,
  method = "fixed", fix_alpha = FALSE, alpha_max = 1
)
summary(fit_two)
mean_difference <- fit_two$posterior_treatment$posterior_mu -
  fit_two$posterior_control$posterior_mu
mean_interval <- quantile(mean_difference, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The historical control weight is `r round(fit_two$posterior_control$alpha_discount, 4)`, compared with `r round(fit_two$posterior_treatment$alpha_discount, 4)` for treatment. The posterior median treatment-minus-control difference is `r round(median(mean_difference), 4)` score units, with a 95% credible interval from `r round(mean_interval[1], 4)` to `r round(mean_interval[2], 4)`. The interval lies above zero, supporting a positive effect under this analysis. Whether that effect is beneficial or clinically important depends on the score definition and a prespecified meaningful difference.

```{r mean-difference, fig.cap="Posterior treatment-minus-control mean difference, with zero marked by the dashed line.", fig.alt="Posterior treatment-minus-control mean difference, with zero marked by the dashed line."}
plot(fit_two, type = "effect")
```

# Sensitivity to the weighting method

```{r mc-comparison}
set.seed(42)
fit_mc <- bdpnormal(
  mu_t = 45, sigma_t = 10, N_t = 50,
  mu0_t = 50, sigma0_t = 10, N0_t = 50,
  method = "mc", fix_alpha = FALSE, alpha_max = 1
)
knitr::kable(rbind(
  "Historical weight" = quantile(fit_mc$posterior_treatment$alpha_discount, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),
  "Population mean" = quantile(fit_mc$posterior_treatment$posterior_mu, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
), digits = 4)
```

The draw-specific calculation mixes over generated weights. It is not merely a less precise estimate of the fixed-weight result. Compare the outcome summaries as well as the weight distribution, and increase `number_mcmc` to assess numerical stability.

# Model and computation

For each source, assume independent normal observations and the baseline prior $p(\mu,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2$. Let $\bar y,s,N$ be the current sample mean, SD, and size. The separate current-data posterior is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde\sigma^2\mid\text{data}&\sim\operatorname{InverseGamma}\left(\frac{N-1}{2},\frac{(N-1)s^2}{2}\right),\\
\tilde\mu\mid\tilde\sigma^2,\text{data}&\sim\mathcal N(\bar y,\tilde\sigma^2/N).
\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse-gamma convention has density proportional to $x^{-a-1}\exp(-b/x)$ for shape $a$ and scale $b$. Replace the statistics by $\bar y_0,s_0,N_0$ for the historical posterior, with draws $\mu_0,\sigma_0^2$. These are posterior distributions of population parameters, not predictive distributions for a new observation [@gelman2013].

For a fixed estimated weight, use $q=\Pr(\tilde\mu<\mu_0\mid\text{data})$ and $p=2\min(q,1-q)$. The draw-specific method instead uses

$$
Z_s=\frac{|\tilde\mu^{(s)}-\mu_0^{(s)}|}
{\sqrt{\tilde\sigma^{2(s)}/N+\sigma_0^{2(s)}/N_0}},
\qquad p_s=2\{1-\Phi(Z_s)\}.
$$

Here $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF, and the variance terms are conditional variances of the mean draws. Apply the chosen discount function to obtain $\alpha$ or $\alpha_s$.

For given variance draws and weight, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_s &= \left(\frac{N}{\tilde\sigma^{2(s)}}+
\frac{\alpha_s N_0}{\sigma_0^{2(s)}}\right)^{-1},\\
M_s &= V_s\left(\frac{N\bar y}{\tilde\sigma^{2(s)}}+
\frac{\alpha_s N_0\bar y_0}{\sigma_0^{2(s)}}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The implementation draws $\mu^{(s)}\sim\mathcal N(M_s,V_s)$, setting $\alpha_s=\alpha$ for the fixed method. The reported distribution averages over the sampled variances and, under `"mc"`, weights. It is therefore a mixture of conditional normals, not a single marginal normal distribution. This precision-weighted calculation follows the normal borrowing construction described by @haddad2017; it does not fit one pooled common-variance model.

Without historical data, the marginal posterior of the mean is Student-$t$ with $N-1$ degrees of freedom, location $\bar y$, and scale $s/\sqrt N$. Its equal-tailed credible limits coincide with the usual one-sample $t$ interval under these assumptions; the function does not conduct a one-sample hypothesis test.

# Assumptions and checks

Check the normal approximation, independence, common outcome units, and comparable analysis populations. Summary inputs cannot reveal outliers, clustering, or changes in the distributional shape. Use [linear regression](bdplm-vignette.html) when covariate adjustment is needed. Assess sensitivity to historical weights and variance differences; a small weight should not be interpreted as a posterior probability that the studies are incompatible.
